{
  "measurements": [
    {
      "statistic": "concordance rate",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "preclinical drug versus food choice procedures results with human laboratory drug self-administration studies and double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trials",
      "compared": "preclinical drug versus food choice procedures vs. human laboratory drug self-administration studies and clinical trials",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "In particular, preclinical drug versus food ‘choice’ procedures have produced increasingly concordant results with both human laboratory drug self-administration studies and double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trials."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "concordance",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "preclinical drug versus food choice procedures evaluating subchronic pharmacological treatments with human laboratory drug self-administration studies and double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials for cocaine, opioids, and methamphetamine",
      "compared": "preclinical drug vs. food choice procedures vs. human laboratory drug self-administration studies and clinical trials",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Preclinical drug versus food choice procedures evaluating subchronic pharmacological treatments have produced concordant results with both human laboratory drug self-administration studies and double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials for cocaine [16], opioids [53], and methamphetamine [54]."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "concordance",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "pharmacological treatment results in preclinical drug versus food choice procedures with pharmacological treatment results in the clinical setting",
      "compared": "preclinical drug vs. food choice procedures vs. clinical trials",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Overall, the results of this single clinical trial support the translational concordance between pharmacological treatment results in preclinical drug versus food choice procedures and pharmacological treatment results in the clinical setting."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "concordance",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "pharmacological treatment results in preclinical drug versus food choice procedures with pharmacological treatment results in the clinical setting",
      "compared": "preclinical drug vs. food choice procedures vs. clinical trials",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Overall, these clinical results support the translational concordance between pharmacological treatment results in preclinical drug versus food choice procedures."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "consistency",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "preclinical results with human laboratory studies demonstrating dose-dependent increases in the choice of abused drugs relative to choice of a nondrug alternative",
      "compared": "preclinical drug vs. nondrug choice procedures vs. human laboratory studies",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Second, these preclinical results are consistent with human laboratory studies demonstrating dose-dependent increases in the choice of the abused drugs cocaine [32,33], methamphetamine [34,35], opiates [36], Δ-9tetrahydrocannabinol [37], and tobacco cigarettes [38] relative to choice of a nondrug alternative (usually money)."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "consistency",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "preclinical results with human laboratory data where cocaine users could choose between hypothetical amounts of cocaine and money either immediately or after some delay",
      "compared": "preclinical choice studies vs. human laboratory data",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Furthermore, these preclinical results are also consistent with human laboratory data where cocaine users could choose between hypothetical amounts of cocaine and money either immediately or after some delay [52]."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "consistency",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "preclinical drug versus nondrug choice studies with sex differences in the potency of cocaine to function as a reinforcer under simple schedules of reinforcement",
      "compared": "preclinical drug vs. nondrug choice studies vs. sex differences in cocaine potency",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "The results from these choice studies are generally consistent with sex differences in the potency of cocaine to function as a reinforcer under simple schedules of reinforcement [106,107]."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "correlation",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "morphine withdrawal severity with the probability of chimpanzees choosing morphine over bananas",
      "compared": "morphine withdrawal severity vs. chimpanzee choice",
      "species": [
        "chimpanzees"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "chimpanzees",
      "verbatim": "discovered that behavioral allocation between these two reinforcers was influenced by the state of morphine withdrawal, such that morphine withdrawal severity was positively correlated with the probability of the chimpanzees choosing morphine over bananas."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "correlation",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "morphine withdrawal with increased morphine versus water choice in rats",
      "compared": "morphine withdrawal vs. rat choice",
      "species": [
        "rats"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "rats",
      "verbatim": "Similarly, behavioral allocation between oral morphine and water in rats was influenced by the state of morphine withdrawal, such that morphine withdrawal increased the morphine versus water choice [19]."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "correlation",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "individual differences in baseline behavioral economic ‘demand’ curves for cocaine and an alternative nondrug reinforcer with subsequent baseline cocaine versus nondrug choice",
      "compared": "demand curves for cocaine and food vs. cocaine vs. food choice",
      "species": [
        "rats"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "rats",
      "verbatim": "A recent study in rats reported that individual differences in baseline behavioral economic ‘demand’ curves for cocaine and an alternative nondrug (food pellets or saccharin) reinforcer alone significantly correlated with subsequent baseline cocaine versus nondrug choice [108]."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "concordance",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "preclinical drug versus food choice procedures with human laboratory drug self-administration studies and double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials for cocaine",
      "compared": "preclinical drug vs. food choice procedures vs. human laboratory studies and clinical trials",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Preclinical drug versus food choice procedures evaluating subchronic pharmacological treatments have produced concordant results with both human laboratory drug self-administration studies and double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials for cocaine [16], opioids [53], and methamphetamine [54]."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "concordance",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "d-amphetamine treatment effects on cocaine versus food choice in preclinical studies with clinical trials and human laboratory studies",
      "compared": "d-amphetamine treatment effects (preclinical vs. human vs. clinical)",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Consistent with these clinical trials, d-amphetamine treatment attenuated cocaine versus money choice in human laboratory studies [62,63] and cocaine versus food choice in preclinical studies utilizing both nonhuman primates [14,41,64] and rats [65]."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "concordance",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "pharmacological blockade of KOR with acute administration of nor-BNI or buprenorphine and naltrexone in rats with clinical trial results for cocaine-use disorder",
      "compared": "KOR antagonist treatment (preclinical vs. clinical)",
      "species": [
        "rats"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "rats",
      "verbatim": "Until recently, there were no KOR antagonist clinical treatment results available to provide critical feedback regarding the translatability of these preclinical KOR antagonist results."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "concordance",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "buspirone treatment effects on cocaine versus food choice in nonhuman primates with clinical trial results",
      "compared": "buspirone treatment (preclinical vs. clinical)",
      "species": [
        "nonhuman primates"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "nonhuman primates",
      "verbatim": "Overall, and consistent with the preclinical KOR antagonist treatment results described above, buspirone treatment effects appear to depend upon the schedule of reinforcement."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "concordance",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "other",
      "measures": "preclinical drug versus food choice procedures evaluating the efficacy of treatment strategies with human laboratory studies and clinical trials",
      "compared": "preclinical drug vs. food choice procedures vs. human laboratory studies and clinical trials",
      "species": [],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "Furthermore, preclinical drug versus food choice procedures evaluating the efficacy of both nonpharmacological and pharmacological treatment strategies have produced translationally relevant and concordant results with both human laboratory studies and clinical trials."
